chunks: My father (may God be pleased with him) narrated to us. He said: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Yahya ibn al-Mubarak, from Abdullah ibn Jabala, from Ishaq ibn Ammar. He said: I heard Abu Abdillah al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) say:
There is no prayer for a haqin, nor for a haqib, nor for a haziq.
The haqin is the one who has urine [and must go], the haqib is the one who has stool [and must go], and the haziq is the one whose foot has been constricted by a leather sock.

key_terms.الخف: A leather sock or soft leather footwear worn over the foot, common in classical Islamic legal discussions of prayer and purity
key_terms.حازق: One whose foot is squeezed or constricted by tight footwear; from hazq (squeezing/pressing)
key_terms.حاقب: One who urgently needs to defecate; from haqb (retention of bowel)
key_terms.حاقن: One who urgently needs to urinate but is holding it back; from haqn (restraining liquid)
key_terms.لا صلاة: The negation formula 'there is no prayer' — used in hadith to indicate invalidity or deficiency of the prayer

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to pray when you urgently need to use the bathroom in Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) issues a legal ruling that prayer (salat) is not valid in three circumstances where the worshipper is severely physically distracted: when urgently needing to urinate (haqin), when urgently needing to defecate (haqib), or when wearing footwear so tight it causes pain (haziq). The Imam then defines each technical term for the benefit of the community. This ruling reflects the Islamic principle that prayer requires presence of mind and physical ease — a person in intense discomfort cannot achieve the necessary concentration (khushu') in prayer.
word_analysis: the one whose feet are constricted (haziq)
